title: CTXAgent Self-Controlled Context Management of LLM Agents

paper.title: CTXAgent Self-Controlled Context Management of LLM Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Agent harnesses keep long sessions inside the context window by compacting the history when
a token threshold is crossed. We study an alternative in which the model manages its own
context: it decides when to compact, what to keep and what to write as the hand-off, given
two tools and one paragraph of guidance. Since earlier work found that open-weight models
cannot manage their own context without scaffolding, we compare seven frontier models under
identical conditions, with and without the context tools, on token cost and benchmark score,
and we compare our harness with three widely used harnesses on two of these models. The benchmark
is assembled from existing ones: coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and
SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks are interleaved with planted facts, ephemeral
observations and standing instructions, all checked deterministically, in sessions of
35–212 turns that resemble a user working through different tasks in one chat. Most of the
strongest models manage their context: they compact and curate regularly, the live context
of the mixed sessions stays mostly below 100k tokens, and their benchmark
scores mostly do not drop significantly. For the models that manage their context well, the
cost reduction is substantial but varies between models, because some models compact so
often that other costs increase.
With
Claude Opus 5.5, the self-managed harness matches Claude Code on task success at 34 % lower cost
than its explicit 200k-window configuration and 49 % lower than its default, with no context
window to choose. We release the agent, the benchmark and all result rows.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The dominant cost of a long agent session is the prefix re-sent with every request, and the dominant risk is that the prefix stops fitting or stops being useful, either because the window overflows or because the information that matters is buried among tokens that no longer matter. Production harnesses therefore compact: Claude Code trims old tool results, offloads large ones and, close to the window, replaces the history by a structured summary [ 4 , 3 ] ; Codex compacts server-side at a configured limit and keeps the most recent user messages [ 31 , 32 ] ; OpenCode compacts when its configured window is reached [ 2 ] . In their default configurations the moment of compaction is a token threshold and its content is a fixed recipe. The model, which is the only party that knows that a task has just finished and that the files read for it are no longer needed, is not consulted, and the operator has to choose a window that suits every task at once. Whether the model can take over this decision has been examined for open-weight models. Li et al. [22] gave such models a compaction tool and found that, unprompted, they do not recognise when their own context has degraded; they added a rubric probed at fixed intervals, admission gates and a forced backstop, and noted that frontier models with stronger metacognition may not need them. This paper tests that conjecture on seven current models and separates it from the question it raises next: if a model can manage its context, what does a harness built on that ability change compared with a harness built on a threshold? Model-decided compaction has been proposed in several forms, trained into coding agents [ 25 , 50 , 12 ] , scaffolded with a rubric [ 22 ] , or elicited by exposing the context as a file [ 38 ] . In this study, we add a prompt-only variant of model-managed context: two tools and one paragraph of guidance, without training or scaffolding, in a local agent, ctxagent . We run seven current models under this identical instruction, with and without the tools, on a benchmark that interleaves coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and, in a harder family, SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks with planted facts, ephemeral observations and standing rules, so that information lost to compaction can become a task failure. We further run the same model through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and ctxagent on byte-identical sessions of 35–212 turns behind one accounting proxy, so that dollar cost with prompt-cache accounting can be compared across harnesses at their own windows. The paper reports which models manage their context and how, what the management costs and saves on each provider’s price list, which losses it causes, and what the harness changes for a model that manages its context well.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: The documentation of Claude Code states that it clears older tool outputs first and summarises when the window is near, with a manual /compact command [ 4 , 3 ] ; Liu et al. [24] describe a five-layer pipeline from the source (budget reduction, snipping, a time- and cache-aware microcompaction, context collapse, auto-compaction). Codex compacts when the context reaches a configured limit capped at 90 % of the window, keeps the most recent user messages up to a token budget, and for hosted models uses a server-side compaction endpoint [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] ; on our wire it cut at approximately 145k of an explicit 200k window and at 170–190k of its default. OpenCode compacts when its configured window is reached; an optional pruning pass is off by default, and a model-callable compress tool exists only as a third-party plugin that is not part of the harness as shipped [ 2 , 40 ] . Source-code taxonomies document how widespread the threshold pattern is [ 36 , 6 ] . Two developments are relevant here. Anthropic’s API offers, besides threshold compaction, a compaction-on-demand mode in which the application decides when to compact [ 3 ] , which is the primitive on which a model-decided policy can be built; and practitioner tools have adopted the hand-off idea: Amp replaces compaction by a model-written “handoff” [ 1 ] , and Cline lets the model propose a new_task with a carried-over summary [ 7 ] , without measuring what it costs or saves. Lindenbauer et al. [23] show on SWE-bench that replacing older tool observations by placeholders while keeping reasoning and tool calls matches LLM summarisation’s solve rate at half the cost; Zhang et al. [49] map where that stops helping. Cache economics are a recurring theme: TokenPilot [ 47 ] argues that layout mutation breaks prefix continuity and reports 61–87 % cost reductions from cache-efficient management; CliffCompaction [ 30 ] never summarises a summary, drops rather than rewrites, reports approximately 51 % lower cost on Terminal-Bench against Claude Code’s auto-compaction as a matched-budget baseline, and finds cache reads to be about 78 % of the uncompacted bill; Lumer et al. [26] evaluate caching strategies for long-horizon tasks, and Satish et al. [37] note that fewer tokens do not reliably mean lower cost or latency. Slipstream [ 9 ] and Min et al. [29] validate compaction against trajectory divergence. ctxagent ’s automatic tiers implement the masking and cache-stability ideas (Section 3.1 ); this paper is about the policy above them. Li et al. [22] (SelfCompact) let the model invoke summarisation with a rubric on when to fire and when to suppress; in their agentic search setting admission gates and a backstop at 30 % of the window are added. Evaluated on open-weight models (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, GLM-4.7-Flash, MiniMax-M2.5, MiMo-V2-Flash), it matches fixed-interval summarisation at 30–70 % lower cost, and its limitations section names GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3 Pro as models that may detect context degradation without the rubric, which is the conjecture tested in Section 4.1 . Context as a Tool [ 25 ] , AutoCompact [ 50 ] , SWE-MeM [ 12 ] , Focus [ 43 ] , AgentFold [ 48 ] and Context-Folding [ 39 ] make compaction a model action for coding or web agents, mostly through training. Closest to our setting, Context Language Models [ 38 ] elicit self-managed context zero-shot by exposing the context as a file; current models including GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 5 then surpass SelfCompact, Context-Folding and Codex-style summaries, while a 9B model has limited context-management ability. VISTA [ 46 ] elicits self-managed context by giving the model a dashboard of block sizes, recency and remaining budget; our agent shows the model less: the segment ids of shortened results and the review hint, but no budget. We add to this line a prompt-only variant and two measurements it has not had: the behaviour of seven current models under one byte-identical instruction, and dollar cost with prompt-cache accounting against pinned production harnesses at their own windows. Harness choice is a hidden variable in agent evaluation [ 18 , 51 , 21 ] . Vats and Golev [42] find that the scaffold changes tokens per solved task by up to 40 × \times while pass rates move by 0–8 points, and Ariño de la Rubia and Pafka [5] find more than 20 × \times cost gaps between agents on the same model, mostly through the prompt cache, with run-to-run variance larger than the differences between pairings. Our harness comparison has the same shape, in that cost moves while success does not, and the variance finding bounds what three seeds can establish (Section 5.3 ). Chat-memory benchmarks probe retention without tools [ 45 , 27 , 17 ] ; MemoryArena [ 14 ] and SWE-EVO [ 19 ] make later tasks depend on earlier ones, and LoCoBench-Agent [ 35 ] adds a multi-session retention metric to a single-turn predecessor [ 34 ] . Closest to our probes, Wang et al. [44] find that side constraints survive compaction only about 17 % of the time, and Chen [8] that prohibited tool use rises after compaction; our standing rules are the same kind of probe. Our instrument differs in that compaction events are detected on the wire and every probe is labelled with whether a cut lay between fact and probe, the filler is executable coding work from Aider polyglot [ 13 ] and SciCode [ 41 , 15 ] , and the harnesses are production systems at their own windows. Context-Bench [ 20 ] and Terminal-Bench [ 28 ] are the independent-task references.

sections.heading: 3.1 ctxagent
sections.text: ctxagent is a local agent with a set of standard tools, extended by a set of context-management tools: compact_context(summary, keep_from, keep_ids) archives everything between the system prompt and keep_from and replaces it by one summary segment whose text the model wrote, without a summariser call or additional cost; an index of the archived tool results is appended so that a later recall knows its handle. curate_context(drop=[{id, note}]) lists the unreviewed tool results and lets the model replace the ones it has acted on by its own one-line note; everything not named is kept verbatim. The engine appends a one-line hint to the newest tool result when a review is due (every 25 tool batches, or after 20k new tokens); it never acts on the hint itself. As a backup, a standard automatic compaction is implemented, which acts only as a safety net. The guidance is one paragraph of the system prompt (Appendix A ): the agent manages its context itself and judges what is still relevant; every rewrite invalidates the prompt cache from the cut, so rewriting after every step is to be avoided; compact_context is for task boundaries, when a substantial body of work is finished, and replaces it by a hand-off summary (goal, decisions and why, files changed, results, open issues, segment ids worth recalling); curate_context is for the smaller clutter within a task; facts the user stated and standing instructions must survive both. The paragraph is task-agnostic and the same byte string for every model.

sections.heading: 3.2 Benchmark base datasets
sections.text: Two existing benchmarks provide the tasks. Aider-polyglot exercises [ 13 ] in Python (34), JavaScript (48) and Go (36) are self-contained programming exercises scored by the shipped tests, one per turn; frontier models solve the Python track at 100 %, so the exercises serve as the work between which facts must survive, and each grows the context by 3–7k tokens. SciCode problems [ 41 ] are multi-step scientific coding problems, one step per turn, whose later steps call functions written in earlier turns, so that the conversation is the specification of the later steps. We use the dev split (15 problems, 50 steps), whose reference solutions pass our checker. Four dev steps were passed only twice in 188 attempts across all arms, models and harnesses; their targets depend on choices the prompt leaves open (Appendix B ). They remain in the scripts so that every arm does identical work; the ceiling is 46 of 50 steps. The eleven-step Ewald-summation problem is the hardest chain and recurs in the analysis. The hard sessions draw on three further sources, chosen because the mixed sessions leave the strongest models near the ceiling. Terminal-Bench 4.0 [ 28 ] contains 66 tasks with a median expert estimate of about four hours, each with its own container image and verifier. We use the 22 tasks that run in a single container within the resources of a 16-core host and that the review by Epoch AI [ 11 ] does not flag for scoring defects, and draw nine of them, three per seed, across the software, science, operations, security, hardware and ML categories. SWE-bench Pro [ 10 ] provides repository tasks in Python, Go and JavaScript with hidden tests; from its hard subset of 51 instances we take one Python, one Go and one JavaScript repository per seed, repositories disjoint across seeds, and within a repository the instance with the median instruction length. SciCode-Verified [ 16 ] is the corrected test split of SciCode, from which we take problems of three to five steps, three per seed. Each container task is one turn: the agent works in the task’s own image through docker exec and in the task directory, which is mounted on the host, and the task’s own verifier decides pass or fail.

sections.heading: 3.3 Benchmark assembly
sections.text: The sessions are assembled from these tasks such that evidence passes through the context and later turns depend on earlier ones, with the dependency distance as a controlled variable. This rules out an instrument of independent questions answered by single shell commands, on which accuracy is at ceiling for every harness and no compaction can change a score because no evidence enters the context. Figure 1 : One session script is shared by every arm. Coding exercises and SciCode steps are the filler; facts, ephemeral observations and standing rules are planted among them and probed at controlled distances; the context trajectory is read from the wire so that every probe can be labelled with whether a compaction lay between establishing turn and probe. The arms run the same model id through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and ctxagent behind one logging proxy. Figure 1 shows one session script. Three kinds of dependency edge, each with a deterministic checker, are planted among the filler tasks: stated facts, probed later by a direct question; ephemeral observations, for which the bench writes a file with a random run id, asks the agent to print it, and deletes the file before the next turn, so that only the conversation holds the value; and standing rules (“end every reply with a line REF: <token> ”), checked by regular expression on every later reply. Probe turns instruct the agent to answer from memory, and the agent’s tool calls on probe turns are recorded (zero in every session). Distances are drawn from { 3 , 10 , 25 , 50 , 90 } \{3,10,25,50,90\} (up to 200 in the longest session), every distance at least once per session, and each probe is labelled post hoc with whether a compaction lay between the establishing turn and the probe, from the compactions detected on the wire (a prompt-size drop of more than 25 % and 10k tokens between consecutive requests). Four session families are used. Mixed sessions ( mixdep:34@s , three seeds) contain all 34 Python exercises and 6–7 SciCode problems interleaved in seeded order, 20–23 edges and two rules, 101–115 turns, 188 scored questions, and 32 fact and 32 ephemeral probes per arm. Clean chains are five chats of one or two complete SciCode problems and nothing else, run twice per arm, which give the per-step ceiling without context pressure (Table 3 ). The marathon places everything in one chat: 118 exercises in three languages, all 15 SciCode problems, 21 edges at distances up to 200 and two rules, 212 turns and roughly 1.5M tokens of raw history. The hard sessions ( heavy:s , three seeds with disjoint task sets) interleave three SWE-bench Pro instances, three Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks and three SciCode-Verified problems with seven edges, two rules and three recall probes, which ask from memory for the name of a function written for an earlier SciCode step: 35–36 turns, of which the six container tasks are single turns of up to 100 tool calls. sections.text: Table 2: Harnesses and arms. “native” is the harness’s own window for the model id; 200k is set explicitly. Web access is off by flag or configuration in every harness, stated in an identical prompt preamble, and audited in every transcript (zero hits). harness version windows compaction Claude Code 2.1.301 native, 1M, 200k tool-result trimming; auto-compaction near the window (summary) Codex CLI 0.163.0 native, 1M, 200k server-side compaction at window − 13 -13 k; user messages kept OpenCode 1.19.3 200k auto-compaction when the configured window is reached ctxagent with compaction 2a407b9 1M model-decided ( compact_context , curate_context ); age masking as safety net; deep tier at 0.9 × \times 1M never reached ctxagent without compaction 2a407b9 1M none: engine off, context tools and prompt sections removed (Section 4.1 only) Common to all arms: same model id via OpenRouter, provider pinned (no fallbacks); reasoning effort high; output reserve 20k; 100 iterations and 1500 s per turn (3600 s on the hard sessions); fresh process and configuration per session; order shuffled by seed; never two trials of the same (model, harness) at once; tools aligned by class (files, shell, jobs); ctxagent keeps its context tools additionally. The self-managed harness is compared with the two vendor CLIs, Claude Code and Codex, and the open-source harness OpenCode, each at the windows listed in Table 2 ; the model comparison uses a second ctxagent configuration with the context management switched off as the counterfactual. Every request of every harness passes through one logging proxy that records tokens by class (uncached, cache write, cache read, output) and the provider’s billed cost per request, injects the provider pin, and lets the bench detect compactions and peak context on the wire independently of what a harness reports. Costs are reported at OpenRouter list rates on one price table; sessions that ran on OpenAI’s flex tier are re-priced per request from the same tokens. The harness comparison uses Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol (each vendor CLI with its vendor’s model, the open-source harness and ctxagent with both); the model comparison uses seven models.

sections.heading: 3.5 Metrics and statistics
sections.text: Each turn is scored as tests passed, verifier passed (container tasks), probe correct or rule adhered to. Success is reported over all scored turns and, separately, over the solvable SciCode steps (46 of 50; 80 step turns per arm over the three mixed sessions) and, on the hard sessions, over the SciCode-Verified steps and container tasks (51 per arm), because the exercises and the memory probes are at ceiling for every model and the dependent steps are the part of the instrument on which models and arms differ. Retention is P ⁡ ( probe correct ∣ d , compaction between ) P(\text{probe correct}\mid d,\text{compaction between}) . Cost is reported per session with the token anatomy, compactions per session, peak and mean prompt size, requests, tool calls and wall time. The unit of randomisation is the session; paired comparisons use the same (seed, turn) across arms with exact McNemar tests. Harness errors are excluded and the session is repeated; a cost-cap hit is scored 0 and kept (none occurred).

sections.heading: 4.1 Model comparison
sections.text: To benchmark how well the models can manage their context window, we ran seven models through ctxagent on the three mixed sessions, and five of them on the three hard sessions, in two arms: arm A, in which the model may compact and curate, and arm B, with the context tools removed and the two prompt sections dropped, so that the context grows monotonically. Figure 2 : Context size per request against the user turn for seven models under the identical instruction to manage their own context (arm A, solid blue) and with no context management (arm B, dashed orange), three seeds each. Opus, Sol and Astra cut; Sonnet in one session of three; Fable through many small drops; Haiku and Muse Wonder never. Figure 3 : Mixed sessions, pooled over three seeds. Top: change of arm A (self-managed) against arm B (no context management) per model; blue marks a change in favour of arm A, vermilion one against it. Bottom: the absolute values, arm A (dark) above arm B (light). Left: session cost at list rates. Right: solvable SciCode steps passed out of 80; exercises and memory probes are at ceiling in both arms. The light-blue bars with an asterisk give the cost recomputed with the cache-read price set to a twentieth of the input price, the ratio shared by Opus, Sonnet, Sol and Muse Wonder (on the list, Fable’s cache reads cost a fortieth of its input, Astra’s a tenth). The token anatomy behind the cost change is Figure 10 in the appendix. Figure 4 : Hard sessions: change of arm A against arm B per model, pooled over three seeds, five models. Left: session cost at list rates. Right: SciCode-Verified steps and container tasks (SWE-bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 4.0) passed, taken together (51 per arm); memory items and probes are at ceiling in both arms. Blue marks a change in favour of arm A, vermilion one against it; Fable’s light-blue bar with an asterisk is the cost change at a cache-read price of a twentieth of the input price, as in Figure 3 . The absolute values are Figure 12 and the token anatomy is Figure 11 , both in the appendix. Figure 2 plots the context size of every request against the user turn, three sessions per model and arm. The dashed lines are arm B, in which the context grows monotonically to 230–430k tokens by the end of a session; the solid lines are arm A, with the context tools enabled. Under the same task strings the models differ in whether, when and how often they act. Compact calls are the large drops, where the model replaces its history by a hand-off summary it wrote; curate calls are the smaller and more frequent drops, where it replaces individual tool results it has acted on by one-line notes. Opus compacts three to four times per session with a hand-off summary and curates hardly at all. Sol and Astra mix both tools, roughly every ten turns. All three models compact at around 50k–80k tokens, around a third of the occupancy at which Claude Code or Codex would cut. Fable acts mostly through 46 small curate drops over three sessions and compacts once or twice per session. Sonnet compacted in one session of three, with three cuts at 101–112k, and ran the other two to 212k and 280k without using the tools. Haiku and Muse Wonder never called compact_context in six sessions; their 16 and 38 curate calls shrank the context by a few thousand tokens. Figure 3 shows the change in cost and in SciCode steps for the mixed sessions, and Figure 4 shows the same for the hard sessions. Only these results are shown, because the other tasks, the coding exercises and the recall of earlier facts and observations, are at the ceiling in all cases. The standing rules are followed in more than 99 % of the replies on the mixed sessions, except by Muse Wonder (83 % in arm A, 78 % in arm B), and in 80–99 % on the hard sessions. Based on their behaviour and on the change in cost and score, the models fall into three groups. Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.1 reduce the session cost substantially in both settings, by 16–58 %, while losing only a few percent of the score on the mixed sessions and improving their score on the hard sessions. Astra 6 and Fable 5.1, the flagship models, produce mixed results. Like Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.1, Astra and Fable keep their context very small during the mixed sessions, which leads to cost reductions of 26 % and 17 % at the adjusted cache-read price. The actual costs are strongly affected by the price list: Astra’s cached input costs a tenth of fresh input and Fable’s a fortieth, whereas Opus, Sonnet, Sol and Muse Wonder charge a twentieth, so the cache reads that arm B re-sends with every request weigh twice as much for Astra and half as much for Fable. At list prices, a similar behaviour therefore yields a reduction of around 50 % for Astra and of around 0 % for Fable. However, Astra loses 5 of 80 SciCode steps against arm B (71 against 76), while Fable stays nearly constant. On the hard sessions, in turn, Fable loses 11 % of its score. Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Muse Wonder do not manage their context successfully. Sonnet acts in one session of three: in that session it compacts and saves as Opus does, in the other two it behaves like arm B, for a mean cost ratio of 0.84. Muse Wonder and Haiku use only curate calls, which slow the growth of the context slightly but invalidate parts of the cache with each call. For Haiku the two effects cancel (ratio 0.99). Muse Wonder costs 20 % more; its bill is dominated by provider-side cache misses that occur with no rewrite at all, to which the curate calls add.

sections.heading: 4.2 Harness comparison
sections.text: (a) Context size per request on the mixed sessions (three seeds per arm). Left Opus 5.5 (Claude Code at 200k dashed, OpenCode at 200k dotted, ctxagent solid), right Sol 6.1 (Codex at 200k dashed, OpenCode dotted, ctxagent solid). (b) Each harness arm relative to ctxagent at 1M on the same model, pooled over the three seeds: change in list cost per session (left) and in solvable SciCode steps passed out of 80 (right), including the vendor harnesses at their native and 1M windows and OpenCode at 200k. Blue marks a difference in favour of ctxagent (the arm costs more, or scores lower), vermilion one against it. Figure 5 : Mixed sessions at a fixed model. The threshold harnesses run every session up to their cut (Claude Code at approximately 168k, Codex at approximately 145k of an explicit 200k window); the self-managed arm stays below 100k, with cuts at task boundaries. Figure 6 : Hard sessions: each harness arm at an explicit 200k window relative to ctxagent at 1M (arm A) on the same model, pooled over the three seeds: change in list cost per session (left) and in SciCode-Verified steps and container tasks passed, taken together, 51 per arm (right). Blue marks a difference in favour of ctxagent , vermilion one against it. Figure 7 : Marathon (212 turns): context size per request (left) and cumulative cost at list rates (right); OpenCode at 200k dotted. Figures 5 and 7 show the context trajectories and the cost of the same sessions in every harness; Figures 8 and 9 in the appendix give the numbers. Across all sessions, the harnesses kept every planted fact and ephemeral observation except one, which OpenCode lost with Opus on a hard session. Every harness followed the standing instructions in every reply of the mixed sessions, in more than 99 % on the marathon and in 74–99 % on the hard sessions. Task success is also very similar within a model, the only exception being Codex on the hard sessions. The main difference between the harnesses and models is the cost. Claude Code did not auto-compact at its default window for Opus 5.5: its context reached 277k tokens without a cut, and with the [1m] suffix it grew by 7k instead of 3k per turn, reaching 688k and costing 53 % more for the same answers. At an explicit 200k window it compacts once per mixed session at approximately 168k and five times on the marathon. ctxagent with the same model never exceeded 80k on the mixed sessions: it called compact_context three to four times per session, every time at an exercise or problem boundary, with hand-off summaries of 1–2k tokens. On the marathon it compacted eleven times (median 70k tokens) and peaked at 96k. Cost per mixed session for ctxagent was 34 % below the cheapest tested Claude Code setting and 49 % below the default, at the same number of model requests (233 vs 228). On the hard sessions and the marathon, ctxagent likewise cost around 30 % less than Claude Code. OpenCode at 200k with Opus 5.5 behaves similarly to Claude Code at 200k on the mixed sessions and the marathon. On the hard sessions, it is about a third cheaper than Claude Code, roughly at the level of ctxagent . The ordering reverses for Sol 6.1. Codex at 200k compacts once or twice per mixed session at approximately 145k; ctxagent with Sol compacts about eight times per session at 45–96k tokens, but issues 20 % more requests and writes 2.4 × \times the output tokens. Its hand-off summaries are considerably longer, which eats up the savings: on the mixed sessions it costs 16 % more than Codex at 200k. On the marathon, this behaviour is even stronger: ctxagent produces 5 × \times the output tokens of Codex and costs $26.29 against $12.14. Opus, at twice Sol’s per-token price, is the cheaper model in ctxagent on both the mixed sessions and the marathon. OpenCode at 200k with Sol 6.1 also compacts at its threshold like Codex at 200k, but costs 21 % more on the mixed sessions and 53 % more on the marathon. On the hard sessions, it scores about 25 % higher than Codex, the same as ctxagent .

sections.heading: 5.1 Dependence on the model
sections.text: Li et al. [22] found that open-weight models need scaffolding with a rubric, gates and a backstop to control their compaction. Section 4.1 gives the corresponding picture for a set of current frontier models without that scaffolding and shows that the context-management capabilities of the models vary considerably. Some models do not use the tools at all or use them inefficiently, while others achieve gains from them. Optimal context management requires using the right tool at the right time, applying it to the right parts of the context window, and writing precise summaries that keep the important information and leave out the redundant. To help with the timing, the models receive hints that are not mandatory; the decision when to compact and curate remains theirs. Most models compact much more often than a harness with a 200k window would and still achieve competitive scores, which shows that their summaries are precise enough. However, some models do not compact at all: Haiku 5.5 and Muse Wonder only curate, and not enough to reduce the context significantly. Other models compact so often that the resulting cache invalidation shrinks the cost reduction. A further failure mode is that Sol 6.1 writes very extensive summaries, which increase its output tokens by up to a factor of five. Even so, apart from Muse Wonder on the mixed sessions and Sonnet 5.5 on the hard sessions (15 % more at the same score), none of these inefficiencies led to a significant cost increase, nor to a significant drop in benchmark score without a cost reduction of at least similar size. The strongest model in this study, Claude Opus 5.5, managed its context window and reduced its cost significantly while keeping its benchmark scores at the same level on average.

sections.heading: 5.2 ctxagent against other harnesses
sections.text: To analyse how a simple harness with agent-steered context management performs against three widely used harnesses, we compared ctxagent in different settings with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. Again, the results depend on the underlying model, because different models interact differently with the same system prompt and the same set of tools. This becomes visible in the comparison of ctxagent with OpenCode on Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.1: Opus appears to benefit considerably from ctxagent , with a cost reduction of more than a third on the mixed sessions and the marathon, while with Sol, ctxagent and OpenCode stay roughly on par except on the marathon. In general, ctxagent with the context tools achieves about the same benchmark results as the baselines. With Claude Opus 5.5, it reduces the cost by 30 % on average against the baselines with a 200k window, at about the same benchmark score. Opus 5.5 often reduced its cost to approximately Sol’s level, despite twice the per-token price. This shows how much impact intelligent context management can have.

sections.heading: 5.3 Limitations
sections.text: The results vary strongly, especially where the models decide themselves when and how to compact and curate. Because of the cost, the number of benchmark runs was very limited, so further, more thorough benchmarking is needed. The system prompt has not been optimised yet. Instructions that steer the models’ compaction and curation behaviour will likely improve the results further, especially when tailored to the specific model. Each vendor CLI was run with its vendor’s model, so harness and model are confounded in the cross-vendor cost comparison. Ariño de la Rubia and Pafka [5] report run-to-run cost variance on the same model and harness that can exceed differences between harnesses: the Opus cost differences here are far outside the seed spread on the mixed sessions (every ctxagent seed below every Claude Code seed in each window condition), whereas the success differences are not significant. The memory instrument was at or near ceiling for every arm; it bounds retention from below but does not rank harnesses on it. Costs are list prices from one provider on one date, and the cache-economics argument concerns ratios that vendors can change.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this study, we examined which language models can manage their own context in agentic coding sessions and compared a harness built on that ability with three popular harnesses. The models received two tools to manage their context: a compaction tool that condenses most of the context at once and a curation tool for smaller operations. They received no extensive instructions on how and when to use them, only one short paragraph of broad guidance. We ran seven current models on identical tasks with and without the tools, and ran the same model through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and our agent ctxagent on identical sessions of 35–212 turns, with planted facts, ephemeral observations, standing rules, dependent SciCode steps and tasks from Terminal-Bench 4.0 and SWE-bench Pro. The models differ considerably in their ability to use the compaction and curation tools. Among the seven frontier models, only GPT-6.1 Sol by OpenAI and Claude Opus 5.5 by Anthropic achieved a relatively consistent gain in benchmark score per cost by managing their context themselves. Most other models did not get worse in cost per score, but did not achieve consistent, significant gains either. The harness comparison showed that our harness ctxagent is on average at least on par with the other tested harnesses, but the results vary. Relative to the other three harnesses, Opus 5.5 appears to work better with ctxagent than Sol 6.1 does. The cost reductions of Opus with ctxagent relative to Claude Code and OpenCode are around 30 % or more in most settings, while Sol with ctxagent mostly stays at the level of the other harnesses. Whether agent-steered context management benefits task success and cost depends on the model. Under the same instruction, the models behaved differently, ranging from no context management to too frequent management. Among the current frontier models, Opus 5.5 gained most consistently from the context-management tools. GPT-6.1 Sol also improved with the tools enabled, but over long sessions it worked less well and less consistently with our harness than with Codex and OpenCode. Further benchmarking is needed, as the results still vary strongly and these benchmarks only partially reflect how a user actually works with an agent. The gains can probably be increased further by optimising the prompt.

sections.heading: Appendix A The context-management guidance
sections.text: The paragraph of ctxagent ’s system prompt that constitutes the self-management policy, verbatim (it follows the generic tool guidelines and a paragraph explaining that shortened tool output carries a segment_id and can be restored with recall ): Managing your own context You manage your context yourself: judge what is still relevant to the work ahead and act on it; the harness only masks old results by age as a safety net. Every rewrite invalidates the prompt cache from the cut, so do not rewrite after every step. compact_context is for task boundaries: when a substantial body of work is finished and the next work does not need its details, replace it by a handoff summary (goal, decisions and why, files changed, results, open issues, segment ids worth recalling). curate_context is for the smaller clutter within a task: when the harness hints that a review is due, or a step left a lot of dead output, drop what you have already acted on with a one-line takeaway. Facts the user stated and standing instructions must survive both. Three tool-choice lines are part of the same prompt: “run_command for anything that finishes within about a minute; start_job for long builds, simulations or servers”; “Pick the reader by size: read_file for a file you can read in one call; summarize_file, focus_file or summarize_folder for large or unfamiliar ones”; and “Every model round trip re-sends the whole context: put independent calls in ONE response. Calls run in order, so an edit and the command that checks it can share one; only a call whose arguments need a result you have not seen yet must wait.” The review hint the engine appends reads “a context review is due; at the next boundary, compact_context(summary=…) is the better tool if the earlier work is finished”. Arm B of Section 4.1 drops this paragraph and the recall paragraph automatically when the engine is off. The prompt preamble prepended to the first user turn of every session in every harness reads: “Work only with the files in the working directory and the tools available to you. Do not access the internet (no web search, no fetching URLs, no package installation, no git clone from remote). If something seems to require it, say so and continue without it.”

sections.heading: Appendix B Unsolvable-as-specified SciCode steps
sections.text: Steps 44.3 ( entropies ), 47.4 ( MC ), 70.8 ( probabilities_3nu ) and 78.3 ( pendulum_analysis ) of the SciCode dev split were attempted 35, 15, 25 and 5 times across the mixed sessions and clean chains by both models in every harness and never passed; in the further 108 attempts of the marathon, the OpenCode sessions and the seven-model comparison, ctxagent -Opus passed 47.4 once in the marathon and Astra passed 70.8 once. The reference solutions pass the checker, so the tests are consistent with one implementation; the failures are value mismatches and, for 78.3, a shape mismatch: the target is a 2 × 2 2\times 2 array while the prompt asks to “output the trajectory” and never states the shape. The common cause is a target that depends on a choice the step description leaves open: the order of random-number draws in a Monte-Carlo energy trace, the time-step selection rule and its metric, the convention for the mixing matrix. The audit log of the SciCode-Verified project [ 16 ] lists all four steps as defects of the dev split: for 44.3 the reference solution overwrites the documented input d0 with a constant, for 47.4 the tests depend on a shared random-number state, for 70.8 the third test is numerically ill-conditioned and the reference solution fails it, and for 78.3 the reference solution selects the time step from the wall clock so that the output shape is machine-dependent. The corrections released with the paper itself [ 15 ] cover only the test split, so no corrected dev steps exist to re-score. Every arm does the same work on these turns; per-step success is reported on the 46 solvable steps.

Cyron 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Simulation in Mechanics, Hamburg University of Technology, Eißendorfer Straße, 21073 Hamburg, Germany Affiliation: Institute of Material Systems Modeling, Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon, Max-Planck-Straße, 21502 Geesthacht, Germany Abstract Agent harnesses keep long sessions inside the context window by compacting the history when a token threshold is crossed. We study an alternative in which the model manages its own context: it decides when to compact, what to keep and what to write as the hand-off, given two tools and one paragraph of guidance. Since earlier work found that open-weight models cannot manage their own context without scaffolding, we compare seven frontier models under identical conditions, with and without the context tools, on token cost and benchmark score, and we compare our harness with three widely used harnesses on two of these models. The benchmark is assembled from existing ones: coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks are interleaved with planted facts, ephemeral observations and standing instructions, all checked deterministically, in sessions of 35–212 turns that resemble a user working through different tasks in one chat. Most of the strongest models manage their context: they compact and curate regularly, the live context of the mixed sessions stays mostly below 100k tokens, and their benchmark scores mostly do not drop significantly. For the models that manage their context well, the cost reduction is substantial but varies between models, because some models compact so often that other costs increase. With Claude Opus 5.5, the self-managed harness matches Claude Code on task success at 34 % lower cost than its explicit 200k-window configuration and 49 % lower than its default, with no context window to choose. We release the agent, the benchmark and all result rows. Keywords: large language models · LLM agents · context management · context compaction · prompt caching · agent harnesses 1 Introduction The dominant cost of a long agent session is the prefix re-sent with every request, and the dominant risk is that the prefix stops fitting or stops being useful, either because the window overflows or because the information that matters is buried among tokens that no longer matter. Production harnesses therefore compact: Claude Code trims old tool results, offloads large ones and, close to the window, replaces the history by a structured summary [ 4 , 3 ] ; Codex compacts server-side at a configured limit and keeps the most recent user messages [ 31 , 32 ] ; OpenCode compacts when its configured window is reached [ 2 ] . In their default configurations the moment of compaction is a token threshold and its content is a fixed recipe. The model, which is the only party that knows that a task has just finished and that the files read for it are no longer needed, is not consulted, and the operator has to choose a window that suits every task at once. Whether the model can take over this decision has been examined for open-weight models. Li et al. [22] gave such models a compaction tool and found that, unprompted, they do not recognise when their own context has degraded; they added a rubric probed at fixed intervals, admission gates and a forced backstop, and noted that frontier models with stronger metacognition may not need them. This paper tests that conjecture on seven current models and separates it from the question it raises next: if a model can manage its context, what does a harness built on that ability change compared with a harness built on a threshold? Model-decided compaction has been proposed in several forms, trained into coding agents [ 25 , 50 , 12 ] , scaffolded with a rubric [ 22 ] , or elicited by exposing the context as a file [ 38 ] . In this study, we add a prompt-only variant of model-managed context: two tools and one paragraph of guidance, without training or scaffolding, in a local agent, ctxagent . We run seven current models under this identical instruction, with and without the tools, on a benchmark that interleaves coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and, in a harder family, SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks with planted facts, ephemeral observations and standing rules, so that information lost to compaction can become a task failure. We further run the same model through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and ctxagent on byte-identical sessions of 35–212 turns behind one accounting proxy, so that dollar cost with prompt-cache accounting can be compared across harnesses at their own windows. The paper reports which models manage their context and how, what the management costs and saves on each provider’s price list, which losses it causes, and what the harness changes for a model that manages its context well. 2 Related work The documentation of Claude Code states that it clears older tool outputs first and summarises when the window is near, with a manual /compact command [ 4 , 3 ] ; Liu et al. [24] describe a five-layer pipeline from the source (budget reduction, snipping, a time- and cache-aware microcompaction, context collapse, auto-compaction). Codex compacts when the context reaches a configured limit capped at 90 % of the window, keeps the most recent user messages up to a token budget, and for hosted models uses a server-side compaction endpoint [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] ; on our wire it cut at approximately 145k of an explicit 200k window and at 170–190k of its default. OpenCode compacts when its configured window is reached; an optional pruning pass is off by default, and a model-callable compress tool exists only as a third-party plugin that is not part of the harness as shipped [ 2 , 40 ] . Source-code taxonomies document how widespread the threshold pattern is [ 36 , 6 ] . Two developments are relevant here. Anthropic’s API offers, besides threshold compaction, a compaction-on-demand mode in which the application decides when to compact [ 3 ] , which is the primitive on which a model-decided policy can be built; and practitioner tools have adopted the hand-off idea: Amp replaces compaction by a model-written “handoff” [ 1 ] , and Cline lets the model propose a new_task with a carried-over summary [ 7 ] , without measuring what it costs or saves. Lindenbauer et al. [23] show on SWE-bench that replacing older tool observations by placeholders while keeping reasoning and tool calls matches LLM summarisation’s solve rate at half the cost; Zhang et al. [49] map where that stops helping. Cache economics are a recurring theme: TokenPilot [ 47 ] argues that layout mutation breaks prefix continuity and reports 61–87 % cost reductions from cache-efficient management; CliffCompaction [ 30 ] never summarises a summary, drops rather than rewrites, reports approximately 51 % lower cost on Terminal-Bench against Claude Code’s auto-compaction as a matched-budget baseline, and finds cache reads to be about 78 % of the uncompacted bill; Lumer et al. [26] evaluate caching strategies for long-horizon tasks, and Satish et al. [37] note that fewer tokens do not reliably mean lower cost or latency. Slipstream [ 9 ] and Min et al. [29] validate compaction against trajectory divergence. ctxagent ’s automatic tiers implement the masking and cache-stability ideas (Section 3.1 ); this paper is about the policy above them. Li et al. [22] (SelfCompact) let the model invoke summarisation with a rubric on when to fire and when to suppress; in their agentic search setting admission gates and a backstop at 30 % of the window are added. Evaluated on open-weight models (Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, GLM-4.7-Flash, MiniMax-M2.5, MiMo-V2-Flash), it matches fixed-interval summarisation at 30–70 % lower cost, and its limitations section names GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3 Pro as models that may detect context degradation without the rubric, which is the conjecture tested in Section 4.1 . Context as a Tool [ 25 ] , AutoCompact [ 50 ] , SWE-MeM [ 12 ] , Focus [ 43 ] , AgentFold [ 48 ] and Context-Folding [ 39 ] make compaction a model action for coding or web agents, mostly through training. Closest to our setting, Context Language Models [ 38 ] elicit self-managed context zero-shot by exposing the context as a file; current models including GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 5 then surpass SelfCompact, Context-Folding and Codex-style summaries, while a 9B model has limited context-management ability. VISTA [ 46 ] elicits self-managed context by giving the model a dashboard of block sizes, recency and remaining budget; our agent shows the model less: the segment ids of shortened results and the review hint, but no budget. We add to this line a prompt-only variant and two measurements it has not had: the behaviour of seven current models under one byte-identical instruction, and dollar cost with prompt-cache accounting against pinned production harnesses at their own windows. Harness choice is a hidden variable in agent evaluation [ 18 , 51 , 21 ] . Vats and Golev [42] find that the scaffold changes tokens per solved task by up to 40 × \times while pass rates move by 0–8 points, and Ariño de la Rubia and Pafka [5] find more than 20 × \times cost gaps between agents on the same model, mostly through the prompt cache, with run-to-run variance larger than the differences between pairings. Our harness comparison has the same shape, in that cost moves while success does not, and the variance finding bounds what three seeds can establish (Section 5.3 ). Chat-memory benchmarks probe retention without tools [ 45 , 27 , 17 ] ; MemoryArena [ 14 ] and SWE-EVO [ 19 ] make later tasks depend on earlier ones, and LoCoBench-Agent [ 35 ] adds a multi-session retention metric to a single-turn predecessor [ 34 ] . Closest to our probes, Wang et al. [44] find that side constraints survive compaction only about 17 % of the time, and Chen [8] that prohibited tool use rises after compaction; our standing rules are the same kind of probe. Our instrument differs in that compaction events are detected on the wire and every probe is labelled with whether a cut lay between fact and probe, the filler is executable coding work from Aider polyglot [ 13 ] and SciCode [ 41 , 15 ] , and the harnesses are production systems at their own windows. Context-Bench [ 20 ] and Terminal-Bench [ 28 ] are the independent-task references. 3 Methods 3.1 ctxagent ctxagent is a local agent with a set of standard tools, extended by a set of context-management tools: compact_context(summary, keep_from, keep_ids) archives everything between the system prompt and keep_from and replaces it by one summary segment whose text the model wrote, without a summariser call or additional cost; an index of the archived tool results is appended so that a later recall knows its handle. curate_context(drop=[{id, note}]) lists the unreviewed tool results and lets the model replace the ones it has acted on by its own one-line note; everything not named is kept verbatim. The engine appends a one-line hint to the newest tool result when a review is due (every 25 tool batches, or after 20k new tokens); it never acts on the hint itself. As a backup, a standard automatic compaction is implemented, which acts only as a safety net. The guidance is one paragraph of the system prompt (Appendix A ): the agent manages its context itself and judges what is still relevant; every rewrite invalidates the prompt cache from the cut, so rewriting after every step is to be avoided; compact_context is for task boundaries, when a substantial body of work is finished, and replaces it by a hand-off summary (goal, decisions and why, files changed, results, open issues, segment ids worth recalling); curate_context is for the smaller clutter within a task; facts the user stated and standing instructions must survive both. The paragraph is task-agnostic and the same byte string for every model. 3.2 Benchmark base datasets Two existing benchmarks provide the tasks. Aider-polyglot exercises [ 13 ] in Python (34), JavaScript (48) and Go (36) are self-contained programming exercises scored by the shipped tests, one per turn; frontier models solve the Python track at 100 %, so the exercises serve as the work between which facts must survive, and each grows the context by 3–7k tokens. SciCode problems [ 41 ] are multi-step scientific coding problems, one step per turn, whose later steps call functions written in earlier turns, so that the conversation is the specification of the later steps. We use the dev split (15 problems, 50 steps), whose reference solutions pass our checker. Four dev steps were passed only twice in 188 attempts across all arms, models and harnesses; their targets depend on choices the prompt leaves open (Appendix B ). They remain in the scripts so that every arm does identical work; the ceiling is 46 of 50 steps. The eleven-step Ewald-summation problem is the hardest chain and recurs in the analysis. The hard sessions draw on three further sources, chosen because the mixed sessions leave the strongest models near the ceiling. Terminal-Bench 4.0 [ 28 ] contains 66 tasks with a median expert estimate of about four hours, each with its own container image and verifier. We use the 22 tasks that run in a single container within the resources of a 16-core host and that the review by Epoch AI [ 11 ] does not flag for scoring defects, and draw nine of them, three per seed, across the software, science, operations, security, hardware and ML categories. SWE-bench Pro [ 10 ] provides repository tasks in Python, Go and JavaScript with hidden tests; from its hard subset of 51 instances we take one Python, one Go and one JavaScript repository per seed, repositories disjoint across seeds, and within a repository the instance with the median instruction length. SciCode-Verified [ 16 ] is the corrected test split of SciCode, from which we take problems of three to five steps, three per seed. Each container task is one turn: the agent works in the task’s own image through docker exec and in the task directory, which is mounted on the host, and the task’s own verifier decides pass or fail. 3.3 Benchmark assembly The sessions are assembled from these tasks such that evidence passes through the context and later turns depend on earlier ones, with the dependency distance as a controlled variable. This rules out an instrument of independent questions answered by single shell commands, on which accuracy is at ceiling for every harness and no compaction can change a score because no evidence enters the context. Figure 1 : One session script is shared by every arm. Coding exercises and SciCode steps are the filler; facts, ephemeral observations and standing rules are planted among them and probed at controlled distances; the context trajectory is read from the wire so that every probe can be labelled with whether a compaction lay between establishing turn and probe. The arms run the same model id through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and ctxagent behind one logging proxy. Figure 1 shows one session script. Three kinds of dependency edge, each with a deterministic checker, are planted among the filler tasks: stated facts, probed later by a direct question; ephemeral observations, for which the bench writes a file with a random run id, asks the agent to print it, and deletes the file before the next turn, so that only the conversation holds the value; and standing rules (“end every reply with a line REF: <token> ”), checked by regular expression on every later reply. Probe turns instruct the agent to answer from memory, and the agent’s tool calls on probe turns are recorded (zero in every session). Distances are drawn from { 3 , 10 , 25 , 50 , 90 } \{3,10,25,50,90\} (up to 200 in the longest session), every distance at least once per session, and each probe is labelled post hoc with whether a compaction lay between the establishing turn and the probe, from the compactions detected on the wire (a prompt-size drop of more than 25 % and 10k tokens between consecutive requests). Four session families are used. Mixed sessions ( mixdep:34@s , three seeds) contain all 34 Python exercises and 6–7 SciCode problems interleaved in seeded order, 20–23 edges and two rules, 101–115 turns, 188 scored questions, and 32 fact and 32 ephemeral probes per arm. Clean chains are five chats of one or two complete SciCode problems and nothing else, run twice per arm, which give the per-step ceiling without context pressure (Table 3 ). The marathon places everything in one chat: 118 exercises in three languages, all 15 SciCode problems, 21 edges at distances up to 200 and two rules, 212 turns and roughly 1.5M tokens of raw history. The hard sessions ( heavy:s , three seeds with disjoint task sets) interleave three SWE-bench Pro instances, three Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks and three SciCode-Verified problems with seven edges, two rules and three recall probes, which ask from memory for the name of a function written for an earlier SciCode step: 35–36 turns, of which the six container tasks are single turns of up to 100 tool calls. Success is reported over all scored turns and, separately, over the solvable SciCode steps (46 of 50; 80 step turns per arm over the three mixed sessions) and, on the hard sessions, over the SciCode-Verified steps and container tasks (51 per arm), because the exercises and the memory probes are at ceiling for every model and the dependent steps are the part of the instrument on which models and arms differ. Retention is P ⁡ ( probe correct ∣ d , compaction between ) P(\text{probe correct}\mid d,\text{compaction between}) . [22] found that open-weight models need scaffolding with a rubric, gates and a backstop to control their compaction. Section 4.1 gives the corresponding picture for a set of current frontier models without that scaffolding and shows that the context-management capabilities of the models vary considerably. Some models do not use the tools at all or use them inefficiently, while others achieve gains from them. Optimal context management requires using the right tool at the right time, applying it to the right parts of the context window, and writing precise summaries that keep the important information and leave out the redundant. To help with the timing, the models receive hints that are not mandatory; the decision when to compact and curate remains theirs. Most models compact much more often than a harness with a 200k window would and still achieve competitive scores, which shows that their summaries are precise enough. However, some models do not compact at all: Haiku 5.5 and Muse Wonder only curate, and not enough to reduce the context significantly. Other models compact so often that the resulting cache invalidation shrinks the cost reduction. A further failure mode is that Sol 6.1 writes very extensive summaries, which increase its output tokens by up to a factor of five. Even so, apart from Muse Wonder on the mixed sessions and Sonnet 5.5 on the hard sessions (15 % more at the same score), none of these inefficiencies led to a significant cost increase, nor to a significant drop in benchmark score without a cost reduction of at least similar size. The strongest model in this study, Claude Opus 5.5, managed its context window and reduced its cost significantly while keeping its benchmark scores at the same level on average. 5.2 ctxagent against other harnesses To analyse how a simple harness with agent-steered context management performs against three widely used harnesses, we compared ctxagent in different settings with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode. Again, the results depend on the underlying model, because different models interact differently with the same system prompt and the same set of tools. This becomes visible in the comparison of ctxagent with OpenCode on Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.1: Opus appears to benefit considerably from ctxagent , with a cost reduction of more than a third on the mixed sessions and the marathon, while with Sol, ctxagent and OpenCode stay roughly on par except on the marathon. In general, ctxagent with the context tools achieves about the same benchmark results as the baselines. With Claude Opus 5.5, it reduces the cost by 30 % on average against the baselines with a 200k window, at about the same benchmark score. Opus 5.5 often reduced its cost to approximately Sol’s level, despite twice the per-token price. This shows how much impact intelligent context management can have. 5.3 Limitations The results vary strongly, especially where the models decide themselves when and how to compact and curate. Because of the cost, the number of benchmark runs was very limited, so further, more thorough benchmarking is needed. The system prompt has not been optimised yet. Instructions that steer the models’ compaction and curation behaviour will likely improve the results further, especially when tailored to the specific model. Each vendor CLI was run with its vendor’s model, so harness and model are confounded in the cross-vendor cost comparison. Ariño de la Rubia and Pafka [5] report run-to-run cost variance on the same model and harness that can exceed differences between harnesses: the Opus cost differences here are far outside the seed spread on the mixed sessions (every ctxagent seed below every Claude Code seed in each window condition), whereas the success differences are not significant. The memory instrument was at or near ceiling for every arm; it bounds retention from below but does not rank harnesses on it. Costs are list prices from one provider on one date, and the cache-economics argument concerns ratios that vendors can change. 6 Conclusion In this study, we examined which language models can manage their own context in agentic coding sessions and compared a harness built on that ability with three popular harnesses. The models received two tools to manage their context: a compaction tool that condenses most of the context at once and a curation tool for smaller operations. They received no extensive instructions on how and when to use them, only one short paragraph of broad guidance. We ran seven current models on identical tasks with and without the tools, and ran the same model through Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and our agent ctxagent on identical sessions of 35–212 turns, with planted facts, ephemeral observations, standing rules, dependent SciCode steps and tasks from Terminal-Bench 4.0 and SWE-bench Pro. The models differ considerably in their ability to use the compaction and curation tools. Among the seven frontier models, only GPT-6.1 Sol by OpenAI and Claude Opus 5.5 by Anthropic achieved a relatively consistent gain in benchmark score per cost by managing their context themselves. Most other models did not get worse in cost per score, but did not achieve consistent, significant gains either. The harness comparison showed that our harness ctxagent is on average at least on par with the other tested harnesses, but the results vary. Relative to the other three harnesses, Opus 5.5 appears to work better with ctxagent than Sol 6.1 does. The cost reductions of Opus with ctxagent relative to Claude Code and OpenCode are around 30 % or more in most settings, while Sol with ctxagent mostly stays at the level of the other harnesses. Whether agent-steered context management benefits task success and cost depends on the model. Under the same instruction, the models behaved differently, ranging from no context management to too frequent management. Among the current frontier models, Opus 5.5 gained most consistently from the context-management tools. GPT-6.1 Sol also improved with the tools enabled, but over long sessions it worked less well and less consistently with our harness than with Codex and OpenCode. Further benchmarking is needed, as the results still vary strongly and these benchmarks only partially reflect how a user actually works with an agent. The gains can probably be increased further by optimising the prompt. Appendix A The context-management guidance The paragraph of ctxagent ’s system prompt that constitutes the self-management policy, verbatim (it follows the generic tool guidelines and a paragraph explaining that shortened tool output carries a segment_id and can be restored with recall ): Managing your own context You manage your context yourself: judge what is still relevant to the work ahead and act on it; the harness only masks old results by age as a safety net. Every rewrite invalidates the prompt cache from the cut, so do not rewrite after every step. compact_context is for task boundaries: when a substantial body of work is finished and the next work does not need its details, replace it by a handoff summary (goal, decisions and why, files changed, results, open issues, segment ids worth recalling). curate_context is for the smaller clutter within a task: when the harness hints that a review is due, or a step left a lot of dead output, drop what you have already acted on with a one-line takeaway. Facts the user stated and standing instructions must survive both. Three tool-choice lines are part of the same prompt: “run_command for anything that finishes within about a minute; start_job for long builds, simulations or servers”; “Pick the reader by size: read_file for a file you can read in one call; summarize_file, focus_file or summarize_folder for large or unfamiliar ones”; and “Every model round trip re-sends the whole context: put independent calls in ONE response. Calls run in order, so an edit and the command that checks it can share one; only a call whose arguments need a result you have not seen yet must wait.” The review hint the engine appends reads “a context review is due; at the next boundary, compact_context(summary=…) is the better tool if the earlier work is finished”. Arm B of Section 4.1 drops this paragraph and the recall paragraph automatically when the engine is off. The prompt preamble prepended to the first user turn of every session in every harness reads: “Work only with the files in the working directory and the tools available to you. Do not access the internet (no web search, no fetching URLs, no package installation, no git clone from remote). If something seems to require it, say so and continue without it.” Appendix B Unsolvable-as-specified SciCode steps Steps 44.3 ( entropies ), 47.4 ( MC ), 70.8 ( probabilities_3nu ) and 78.3 ( pendulum_analysis ) of the SciCode dev split were attempted 35, 15, 25 and 5 times across the mixed sessions and clean chains by both models in every harness and never passed; in the further 108 attempts of the marathon, the OpenCode sessions and the seven-model comparison, ctxagent -Opus passed 47.4 once in the marathon and Astra passed 70.8 once. The reference solutions pass the checker, so the tests are consistent with one implementation; the failures are value mismatches and, for 78.3, a shape mismatch: the target is a 2 × 2 2\times 2 array while the prompt asks to “output the trajectory” and never states the shape. The common cause is a target that depends on a choice the step description leaves open: the order of random-number draws in a Monte-Carlo energy trace, the time-step selection rule and its metric, the convention for the mixing matrix. The audit log of the SciCode-Verified project [ 16 ] lists all four steps as defects of the dev split: for 44.3 the reference solution overwrites the documented input d0 with a constant, for 47.4 the tests depend on a shared random-number state, for 70.8 the third test is numerically ill-conditioned and the reference solution fails it, and for 78.3 the reference solution selects the time step from the wall clock so that the output shape is machine-dependent. The corrections released with the paper itself [ 15 ] cover only the test split, so no corrected dev steps exist to re-score. Every arm does the same work on these turns; per-step success is reported on the 46 solvable steps.
